families.title: Clockwork Gates stars
families.mathematics: Hopping k places around n evenly spaced dots and drawing each hop as a straight line splits the dots into gcd(n, k) pieces, each a star or polygon through n / gcd(n, k) dots: the orbits of x ↦ x + k in the cyclic group of order n are the cosets of the subgroup generated by gcd(n, k). One hop reaches every dot exactly when n and k share no factor, so every hop draws a single piece exactly when n is prime. Hop k and hop n − k draw the same picture, and a piece of hop k on n dots is the star polygon {m/j} with m = n / gcd(n, k) and j = k / gcd(n, k).
rules: A hop of k draws a straight line to the dot k places clockwise.
Keep hopping until the line comes back, then start again at a dot with no line.
The drawing is finished when every dot has a line. Each start makes one piece.

sources.title: Bellingham Math Circle — Week 4: Stars and code wheels, packets, return visit and adult guides
H. S. M. Coxeter — Regular Polytopes (1973), §2.8 on star polygons {n/k}
Subgroups and cosets of the cyclic group ℤ/n: the orbits of x ↦ x + k are the cosets of the subgroup generated by gcd(n, k)

puzzles.idea: Hop 2 on 5 dots reaches every dot and draws a five-pointed star.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count to 2 along a ring. Nothing to read.
hints: Tap any dot. Then count 2 dots clockwise and tap where you land.
Keep hopping 2 until you are back where you started.
One start is enough: every dot gets a line.

parent.notice: Whether your child counts the next dot as “one”, not the dot the pen is on.
parent.prompt: Did every dot get a line before you came back?
parent.explanation: Hop 2 on 5 dots lands on 2, 4, 1, 3 and back to 0, so one start reaches every dot. The picture is the star polygon {5/2}.
parent.extension: Which hops on 5 dots come back early?
parent.connection: The orbit of 0 under adding 2 in the cyclic group of order 5 is the whole group, because 2 and 5 share no factor.

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 whole-group launch: hop 2 on a ring of 5.

puzzles.idea: Hop 2 on 6 dots comes back early, so the drawing needs a second start: two triangles.
hints: Hop 2 until the line comes back. Do some dots still have no line?
Start again at a dot with no line, and hop 2 again.
Two starts, two triangles.

parent.notice: Whether your child finds the empty dots and starts again without being told.
parent.prompt: Why did the line come back before reaching every dot?
parent.explanation: Hop 2 on 6 dots only lands on 0, 2 and 4, so the other three dots need a second start. 2 and 6 share the factor 2, and there are 2 pieces.
parent.extension: Which hops on 6 dots need only one start?
parent.connection: The orbits of adding 2 are the cosets of the subgroup {0, 2, 4}: the even and the odd dots.

puzzles.title: Two pieces on eight
puzzles.objective: Choose a hop by drawing the first line, then keep hopping until every dot has a line. Finish with exactly 2 pieces.
puzzles.instruction: Choose a hop by drawing the first line, then keep hopping until every dot has a line. Finish with exactly 2 pieces.
puzzles.controls: Tap a dot to start, then tap another dot: that first line sets the hop. Keep tapping where the hop lands, counting clockwise. When the line comes back, tap a dot with no line to start again. Again clears the drawing and the hop; Undo takes back one tap.
rules: A hop of k draws a straight line to the dot k places clockwise.
Keep hopping until the line comes back, then start again at a dot with no line.
The drawing is finished when every dot has a line. Each start makes one piece.
puzzles.idea: On 8 dots, hops 2 and 6 make 2 pieces; the other hops make 1 or 4.
hints: Your first line sets the hop. Try a hop and see how many starts it needs.
Hops 1, 3, 5 and 7 need one start. Try an even hop.
Hop 2 makes two squares.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts before drawing after a try or two.
parent.prompt: Which hops needed only one start? Which needed more?
parent.explanation: On 8 dots, hops 1, 3, 5 and 7 reach every dot; hops 2 and 6 make two squares; hop 4 makes four lines. The number of pieces is the biggest number that goes evenly into both 8 and the hop.
parent.extension: Can you predict the number of pieces for hop 6 before drawing it?
parent.connection: The number of pieces is gcd(8, k).

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 2–3 Problem 1 (8 dots, hops 1 to 4), turned around: the number of pieces is given.

puzzles.title: Three pieces on twelve
puzzles.objective: Choose a hop by drawing the first line, then keep hopping until every dot has a line. Finish with exactly 3 pieces.
puzzles.instruction: Choose a hop by drawing the first line, then keep hopping until every dot has a line. Finish with exactly 3 pieces.
puzzles.controls: Tap a dot to start, then tap another dot: that first line sets the hop. Keep tapping where the hop lands, counting clockwise. When the line comes back, tap a dot with no line to start again. Again clears the drawing and the hop; Undo takes back one tap.
rules: A hop of k draws a straight line to the dot k places clockwise.
Keep hopping until the line comes back, then start again at a dot with no line.
The drawing is finished when every dot has a line. Each start makes one piece.
puzzles.idea: Three pieces on 12 dots needs a hop that 3 goes into but 6 and 4 don’t: 3 or 9.
hints: Each piece has the same number of dots. How many dots would each of 3 pieces have?
Each piece needs 4 dots: a square.
Hop 3 makes three squares.

parent.notice: Whether your child reasons from the size of a piece (12 ÷ 3 = 4 dots) rather than trying every hop.
parent.prompt: If there are 3 pieces, how many dots does each one have?
parent.explanation: All pieces are turned copies of the first, so 3 pieces on 12 dots have 4 dots each. Hop 3 lands on 0, 3, 6, 9: a square. Hop 9 draws the same squares backward. Hop 6 makes 6 pieces, and hops 2 and 4 make 2 and 4.
parent.extension: On 12 dots, which numbers of pieces are possible?
parent.connection: The pieces are cosets of a subgroup, so they all have the same size, and that size divides 12 (Lagrange’s theorem in its smallest form).

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 2–3 Problem 3 and grades 4–5 Problem 1 (12 dots, hops 1 to 6), turned around.

puzzles.idea: Every even hop except 10 makes 2 pieces on 10 dots: two pentagons or two five-pointed stars.
hints: How many dots does each of 2 pieces have?
Each piece has 5 dots. Try an even hop.
Hop 4 makes two five-pointed stars.

parent.notice: Whether your child notices that hops 2 and 4 both work but draw different pictures.
parent.prompt: Do all the even hops draw the same picture?
parent.explanation: Hops 2, 4, 6 and 8 share the factor 2 with 10 and no bigger one, so each makes 2 pieces of 5 dots. Hops 2 and 8 draw two pentagons; hops 4 and 6 draw two stars {5/2}.
parent.extension: On 10 dots, which hop makes 5 pieces?
parent.connection: gcd(10, k) = 2 for k = 2, 4, 6, 8. Each piece is {5/(k/2)}.

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 2–3 Problem 2 (10 dots, hops 2 to 5), turned around.

puzzles.idea: Hop 6 makes 3 pieces on rings that 3 goes into but 2 doesn’t: 9 and 15.
hints: Hop 6 on 12 dots makes 6 pieces. What would make it 3?
The ring needs 3 as a factor, but not 2.
Try 9 dots.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries rings at random or looks for a ring that 3 goes into.
parent.prompt: What do 6 and the ring have to share?
parent.explanation: Hop 6 on n dots makes gcd(n, 6) pieces. That is 3 exactly when 3 divides n and 2 doesn’t: 9 and 15 among 7 to 16.
parent.extension: With hop 6, which rings make 2 pieces?

puzzles.idea: Eight points and one piece: 8 dots, hop 3 (or 5).
hints: Count the points of the star. How many dots does the ring need?
It is one piece through 8 dots. Which hops on 8 make one piece?
Hop 3 on 8 dots.

parent.notice: Whether your child counts points to choose the ring first.
parent.prompt: How many dots did the picture use? How many pieces does it have?
parent.explanation: The star has 8 points and is one piece, so it uses 8 dots and a hop that shares no factor with 8. Hop 1 draws the octagon and hop 3 the star {8/3}; hop 5 draws the same star backward.
parent.extension: Is there a star with 6 points drawn in one piece?

puzzles.objective: Choose a ring of dots. Draw hop 8 until every dot has a line, and finish with exactly 4 pieces.

puzzles.idea: Hop 8 makes 4 pieces when 4 goes into the ring but 8 doesn’t: 12 and 20.
hints: What must 8 and the ring share for 4 pieces?
The ring needs 4 as a factor, but not 8.
Try 12 dots.

parent.notice: Whether your child rules out 16 (8 pieces) without drawing it.
parent.prompt: Why does 16 give too many pieces?
parent.explanation: Hop 8 on n dots makes gcd(n, 8) pieces: 4 exactly when n is a multiple of 4 but not of 8, so 12 and 20 among 9 to 20. On 12 dots each piece is a triangle; on 20 dots each is a five-pointed star.
parent.extension: On 20 dots, hop 8 draws four stars. Which other hop on 20 draws the same picture?
parent.connection: gcd(n, 8) = 4 for n = 12, 20; on 20 dots the pieces are {5/2}.

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 4–5 Problems 2–3 (how many pieces, without drawing), turned around. New instance.

puzzles.title: Two stars
puzzles.objective: Draw the picture on the card. Choose a ring, then a hop, and draw until every dot has a line.

puzzles.idea: Two five-pointed stars: 10 dots, and a hop that makes 2 pieces with a jump of 2 inside each star.
hints: How many pieces? How many points on each?
Two pieces of 5 points need 10 dots. Which hops on 10 make 2 pieces?
Hop 4 on 10 dots.

parent.notice: Whether your child separates the two questions: how many dots, then which hop.
parent.prompt: Hops 2 and 4 both make 2 pieces on 10 dots. Which one draws stars?
parent.explanation: Two pieces of 5 points use 10 dots, so the hop shares exactly 2 with 10: 2, 4, 6 or 8. Inside each piece the hop jumps k ÷ 2 points of a 5-point ring, so hop 2 draws pentagons and hop 4 (or 6) draws stars.
parent.extension: Draw three five-pointed stars. How many dots, and which hop?
parent.connection: Hop k on n dots draws gcd(n, k) copies of {m/j}, with m = n / gcd(n, k) and j = k / gcd(n, k).

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 4–5 Problem 9 (erased drawings: find the dots and the hop). New instance.

puzzles.idea: Three five-pointed stars: 15 dots and hop 6 (or 9).
hints: How many pieces, and how many points on each?
Three stars of 5 points use 15 dots. Inside each star the hop jumps 2 points.
Hop 6 on 15 dots.

parent.notice: Whether your child uses puzzle 9’s reasoning: 3 × 5 dots, then 3 × 2 for the hop.
parent.prompt: How far does the hop go inside one star? How far is that on the whole ring?
parent.explanation: Three pieces of 5 points use 15 dots, so gcd(15, k) = 3 and k = 3, 6, 9 or 12. Inside each piece the hop jumps k ÷ 3 points of a 5-point ring: 1 for a pentagon (k = 3 or 12), 2 for a star (k = 6 or 9).
parent.extension: Which pictures on 15 dots have exactly 5 pieces?
parent.connection: Compound star figures: gcd(n, k) rotated copies of {m/j}.

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 4–5 Problem 9 (erased drawings), at a size where trying every hop is slow. New instance.

puzzles.title: Every one-piece hop
puzzles.objective: Tap every hop that draws one piece on this ring, then Check.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Tap every hop that makes one piece.
puzzles.instruction: Tap every hop that draws one piece on this ring, then Check.
puzzles.controls: Tap every number that belongs, then Check. You get one check; after a miss, Next brings a new question.
rules: A hop of k draws a straight line to the dot k places clockwise.
Keep hopping until the line comes back, then start again at a dot with no line.
The drawing is finished when every dot has a line. Each start makes one piece.
You get one check per question. After a miss, the answer is shown and Next brings a different question.
puzzles.idea: A hop makes one piece exactly when it shares no factor with the number of dots.
puzzles.prerequisites: Stars puzzles 1–8. Knowing small factors helps.
hints: Which numbers go evenly into the number of dots?
A hop that shares any of those factors comes back early.
Keep only the hops that share no factor with the dots.

parent.notice: Whether your child crosses off multiples of each factor rather than imagining each drawing.
parent.prompt: How can you tell, without drawing, that hop 9 on 30 dots comes back early?
parent.explanation: Hop k on n dots makes gcd(n, k) pieces, so one piece means gcd(n, k) = 1. On 30 dots that leaves 1, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29: eight hops, which is φ(30). There is one check per ring; after a miss the answer is shown and Next brings a different ring.
parent.extension: On 30 dots, how many hops make exactly 2 pieces?
parent.connection: The hops that make one piece are the generators of the cyclic group of order n; there are φ(n) of them (Euler’s totient).

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 4–5 Problems 3 and 7 (the rule for the number of pieces), asked at a size where drawing every hop is slow; idea from docs/insight-without-ai.md (“tap every jump that visits all 30 places”).

puzzles.idea: Every hop makes one piece exactly when the number of dots is prime.
hints: On 12 dots, which hop comes back early? What about 13 dots?
A ring fails if some smaller hop shares a factor with it.
Keep the rings whose only factors are 1 and themselves.

parent.notice: Whether your child connects “some hop comes back early” with “the number of dots can be split evenly”.
parent.prompt: Why does 15 fail? Which hop shows it?
parent.explanation: If n has a factor d between 1 and n, hop d comes back after n ÷ d hops, before reaching every dot. If n is prime, every hop from 1 to n − 1 shares no factor with n. So the rings are exactly the primes: 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19 between 4 and 20.
parent.extension: Week 4 grades 4–5 Problem 8 asks you to explain why your list is complete. Can you?
parent.connection: The cyclic group of order n has no subgroups other than itself and {0} exactly when n is prime.

puzzles.provenance: Week 4 grades 4–5 Problem 8 (rings from 4 to 20 where every hop reaches every dot), with two further ranges for later rounds.
